items.title: Could AI dependence spread from person to person like a virus?
items.description:
Could AI dependence spread from person to person like a virus?

Researchers built a mathematical model separating people into three groups: independent thinkers, AI users who retain their skills, and people who depend on AI to do the thinking.

The model explores a feedback loop: more AI use means less practice, weaker independent skills, and greater reliance on AI. Meanwhile, the advantages of using AI encourage others to adopt it.

The concerning part is the tipping point: once dependence becomes established, reducing AI use may not restore the skills people started with.

items.title: AI has a single point of failure.
items.description:
AI has a single point of failure.

Everyone thinks NVIDIA makes the chips that power AI models like ChatGPT.

But here’s the plot twist: NVIDIA only designs them.

The chips themselves, the brains of modern AI, are actually manufactured by one company in Taiwan called TSMC.

TSMC builds over 90% of the world’s most advanced AI semiconductors, including those inside NVIDIA’s H100 GPUs.

If anything happens to Taiwan, the entire global AI industry could crash overnight.

The scary part?

China claims Taiwan as its own territory… and some reports say they could move in by 2027.

If that happens, it might be the end of the AI industry.

#NVIDIA #

IKEA is one of my favorite examples. They rolled out an AI assistant to handle a share of customer support questions, then moved roughly 8,500 support team members into a brand-new interior design business. That new line reportedly brought in over $1 billion in its first year.

items.title: I talk to AI 50+ times a day, and I'm more sure than ever that voice is where this is all heading.
items.description:
I talk to AI 50+ times a day, and I'm more sure than ever that voice is where this is all heading. 

On the flip side: some AI tools reportedly only need about three seconds of someone's audio to copy their voice.

So my family and I picked a safe word (in person, like it's 1995). It won't stop every scam, but it gives anyone who gets a panicked "it's me, I need money" call one clean question to ask before they send a cent.

The rest of my AI security habits are a lot less dramatic (passkeys, data-sharing opt-outs, and no AI buying anything without checking with me first).

items.description:
I spoke to the CEO of a $10B+ company whose employees were getting calls from scammers pretending to be him. His fix was to give his personal number to EVERY new hire so they can call him directly to verify.

It's the cheapest kind of security there is.

It also means I don't think just recognizing a voice counts as proof anymore. Faking one using AI voice tools has gotten so cheap and accessible that the check has to happen somewhere a clone can't follow, like a number already saved in your phone, a face on FaceTime, or a word only your people know.

items.description:

items.title: The prompt I paste in after I'm done venting to AI about a project:
items.description:
The prompt I paste in after I'm done venting to AI about a project:

"Interview me one question at a time until you understand what I need. Then write a one-page brief and wait for my OK before doing anything."

Before I say OK, I then review the brief and ask myself:

1. Does it know what I want at the end? If it can't say it in one sentence, I probably wasn't clear.
2. Does it know what's off-limits? My budget, my deadline, people it shouldn't email.
3. Does it know when to stop and check with me?
4. Did it get anything wrong? That's usually something I forgot to tell it, so I fix it in the brief.
